title: The Con Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower
paragraphs: In nineteen twenty-five, a man in a perfect suit walked into one of the finest hotels in Paris… and sold the Eiffel Tower. Not a postcard. Not a ticket. The real thing. Seven thousand tons of iron.
And the craziest part? He got away with it. So he came back… and tried to sell it again.
His name was Victor Lustig. He called himself a count. In reality, he was one of the greatest con men who ever lived. And it all started with a boring little newspaper story.

The Eiffel Tower was rusting. Painting and fixing it cost a fortune. It was built for a world's fair in eighteen eighty-nine, and it was only supposed to stand for twenty years. Most readers turned the page. Lustig saw a business opportunity.

First, he forged official government letterhead. Then he gave himself a very important job title. Deputy Director-General of the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs. And he invited the biggest scrap metal dealers in Paris to a secret meeting, at the luxurious Hotel de Crillon.

He told them the city could no longer afford the tower. It would be torn down, and sold for scrap. Seven thousand tons of metal, to the highest bidder. But it had to stay top secret. Imagine the public outcry.
One dealer wanted it more than anyone. His name was André Poisson. Which, funnily enough, is French for fish. And he was about to take the bait.
Poisson was new money. A deal this big would finally make the old families take him seriously. But his wife wasn't so sure. Why all the secrecy? Why the rush?

So Lustig did something brilliant. He confessed. He said government officials were badly paid, and he liked to close his deals quietly. Poisson understood immediately. The official wanted a bribe. And strangely, that made it all feel real.
Poisson paid for the tower, plus a fat bribe on top. Within an hour, Lustig was on a train to Austria, with the money.
Then he waited. Every day, he checked the newspapers. Fraud! Scandal! Arrest! But the story never came. Poisson was too embarrassed to tell anyone he had been fooled.

So Lustig did the unthinkable. He went back to Paris, and tried to sell the Eiffel Tower… again. New dealers. Same pitch. But this time, someone went to the police. Lustig escaped just in time, and sailed for America.
In America, he kept going. He sold a fake money machine, a wooden box that supposedly copied hundred dollar bills. He even conned Al Capone.

He asked Capone for fifty thousand dollars, and promised to double it. Then he locked the cash away for two months, and gave every dollar back, saying the deal had failed. Capone was so impressed by his honesty, he handed Lustig five thousand dollars. Which was the plan all along.

But in nineteen thirty-five, his luck ran out. Agents caught him with fifty-one thousand dollars in fake bills. The day before his trial, he escaped from an escape-proof jail in New York, climbing down a rope made of bedsheets.
He made it as far as Pittsburgh. Twenty-seven days later, he was caught again, and sent to the most famous prison in America. Alcatraz.

Victor Lustig died in federal custody in nineteen forty-seven. And the Eiffel Tower? It's still standing, more than a hundred and thirty years later. Still not for sale. So tell me… would you have bought it?
